title: Practice: Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Mitigations
objective: By the end of this lesson you can name an attack from its symptoms alone, map attacker behaviors onto MITRE ATT&CK tactics, and reach for the mitigation the scenario is pointing at.

blocks.text: Attack questions rarely name the attack. They hand you six facts that smell wrong and wait. The skill being tested is diagnosis: symptom to name, name to mitigation. Both drills below strip away the paragraphs and leave only what a log or a report would show, which is exactly the shape of the exam scenario.
Drill 1: name the attack from six symptoms

rows: Three hundred failed logons in one night, spread across forty different usernames from a single address; three accounts then succeed at 02:40
The finance clerk approves a wire transfer, the request is captured, and the same request is re-sent by someone else at 03:00 and succeeds again
Staff report SMS messages about a missed parcel with a tracking link; the link opens a copy of the bank's login page
A laptop starts long, random-looking DNS queries to one domain every five minutes; nobody on that laptop notices anything
Web server logs show the string ' OR 1=1 -- arriving in the username field of the login form
An invoice arrives from the real supplier's mailbox, but the bank details on it changed last week; the reply-to is a look-alike domain

blocks.title: Diagnose, then act
steps: Name each attack in the table using the vocabulary of the exam: password spraying, replay, smishing, command and control, SQL injection, business email compromise, and near-neighbors you considered and rejected.
For each row, write the one mitigation you would state first, and one neighbor attack it would not stop.
Mark the two rows you would escalate to incident response tonight, and say why those two outrank the rest.
blocks.expected: 1) Password spraying that succeeded three times; first answer is MFA and lockout with timeouts. 2) A replay of a valid request; first answer is TLS plus one-time tokens or nonces. 3) Smishing on a credential-harvest page; first answer is reporting channel plus blocks on the domain, plus awareness training. 4) Command and control beaconing over DNS; first answer is DNS sinkhole and egress filtering. 5) SQL injection; first answer is parameterized queries and input validation, with a WAF as the quick win. 6) Business email compromise; first answer is out-of-band verification of payment changes. Rows 1 and 4 escalate tonight: both mean an actor is already inside operating at scale, while 3 and 6 are attempts at people and can be blocked at the gateway first.

blocks.text: The rejected neighbors are where points hide. Spraying differs from stuffing because the password is guessed across accounts rather than leaked pairs replayed into logins. Replay differs from on-path because the attacker already holds the captured request and no longer needs to sit between the parties. Saying the wrong near-neighbor in your head during practice costs nothing; on the exam it costs the question.
Drill 2: map behaviors to ATT&CK tactics

items: A phishing email with a macro-laden attachment reaches four HR staff.
Two days later, a scheduled task appears on the file server.
A tool attempts to dump the memory of the local security authority process.
The account used on the web server now logs into the database host.
A compressed archive of designs is uploaded to a file-sharing site.

blocks.title: Tactic, not technique
steps: Label each behavior with its MITRE ATT&CK tactic: initial access, persistence, credential access, lateral movement, exfiltration.
For one behavior, also name the technique category in plain words, so the tactic-technique split is visible.
Name the defense that covers the first behavior and one that covers the last.
blocks.expected: Phishing email is initial access. The scheduled task is persistence. The memory dump attempt is credential access. The web-server account on the database host is lateral movement. The upload is exfiltration. The scheduled task's technique category is scheduled task or job. First behavior: email filtering with attachment sandboxing. Last behavior: egress rules and DLP watching large uploads.

blocks.title: Read for the aim
blocks.text: Tactic names the attacker's goal, technique names the method. When a mapping question stalls, ask what the attacker was trying to get or keep at that moment: getting in is initial access, staying in is persistence, harvesting secrets is credential access, moving inward is lateral movement, leaving with the goods is exfiltration.

blocks.title: Lab: Threats Classify
blocks.description: Drag twelve incident summaries into social-engineering, malware, network-attack, and insider bins, including two that skilled defenders argue about. Full design: labs/threats-classify.lab.en.md.

cheatsheet: Spraying guesses a few passwords across many accounts; stuffing replays leaked password pairs; both are answered with MFA and lockout.
Replay sends a captured valid request again; on-path sits between the parties; TLS plus one-time tokens answer both.
Random periodic DNS to one domain is command-and-control beaconing; answer with sinkholes and egress filtering.
Injection strings in input fields point at parameterized queries and a WAF.
ATT&CK tactic names the goal: initial access, persistence, credential access, lateral movement, exfiltration.

checkpoint.prompt: At 03:00, a funds-transfer web request captured two hours earlier is re-sent byte for byte and the bank honors it again. The clerk's session was valid and no attacker is between the bank and the client. What is this?

choices.A: An on-path attack relaying the session
choices.B: A cross-site request forgery using the clerk's browser
choices.C: A replay of a captured valid request
choices.D: A credential-stuffing login using the clerk's password

checkpoint.explanation: The captured request is sent again as-is, with no one positioned between the parties, which defines replay. On-path requires relaying live traffic, CSRF needs the clerk's browser to fire the request, and stuffing is a login attack.

checkpoint.prompt: During a review, an analyst finds a scheduled task created on a server two days after a phishing email was opened. In MITRE ATT&CK terms, which tactic does the scheduled task belong to?
checkpoint.explanation: A scheduled task keeps the attacker's foothold across reboots, which serves the persistence tactic. Initial access was the phishing email two days earlier, and exfiltration has not begun in this scenario.

checkpoint.prompt: Log review shows hundreds of nightly failed logons spread across dozens of usernames from one address, and three accounts that eventually succeed. Which mitigation most directly blunts this campaign?

choices.A: MFA on every account plus lockout with timeouts
choices.D: Blocking all foreign IP addresses at the firewall

checkpoint.explanation: Spraying wins when a right password alone is enough. MFA makes the password insufficient and lockout with timeouts slows the attempt rate. Longer passwords barely raise the cost of a one-guess-per-account spray, and address blocking fails against botnets.
